The spread of leisure sport to women was accelerated by cycling in the 1880s and 1890s and by lawn tennis, which was one of the first sports it was considered socially acceptable for women to play competitively.

Television transformed British sport from the 1950s. The 1953 FA Cup Final was watched by millions on television, demonstrating the medium’s power to bring sport into the home. Advertisers quickly recognised sport as a vehicle for reaching large audiences, and sponsorship grew rapidly. By the 1970s and 1980s, shirt sponsorship had become standard in football; tobacco companies sponsored cricket and racing.

The relationship between sport and television deepened dramatically in 1992 when the English First Division clubs broke away to form the Premier League, selling exclusive broadcast rights to BSkyB (later Sky Sports) for £304 million over five years. This deal transformed football into a multi-billion-pound industry. Player wages soared; overseas players and coaches arrived; clubs became global brands. The 1990s media revolution changed professional sport almost beyond recognition.

Key Fact

The Premier League was formed in 1992 and sold exclusive TV rights to Sky Sports for £304 million. This transformed English football: wages rose sharply, overseas players arrived in large numbers, and clubs became global commercial brands. It is the most-watched football league in the world.

Participation and the Late Twentieth Century

Rising incomes and shorter working hours after the Second World War expanded mass participation in sport and recreation. Golf, which had been largely a middle-class pursuit, became accessible to more people as municipal courses were built. Local authority leisure centres opened from the 1970s, providing swimming pools and sports halls. The running boom of the 1980s and the aerobics craze reflected growing health consciousness. Sport England and similar bodies promoted participation across social groups, though deep inequalities in access by class, gender and ethnicity persisted.

The commercialisation of the Olympics is another example of the tension between sport as amateur competition and sport as commercial spectacle. After the Second World War, the International Olympic Committee gradually relaxed the rules on amateurism; by the 1990s, professional athletes were permitted to compete. Sponsorship and television rights made the Olympics one of the most valuable commercial properties in the world.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Holidays and travel over time
content_html:
Holidays Before the Railway

For most people in medieval and early modern England, holidays meant feast days and holy days. The word “holiday” derives from “holy day”. The Church calendar provided around forty such days per year, including Christmas, Easter, Whitsun and Michaelmas. These were not just religious occasions — they were the primary leisure breaks available to ordinary working people, who filled them with sport, dancing, fairs and communal feasting.

Travel for leisure was a privilege of the wealthy. In the eighteenth century, upper-class young men undertook the Grand Tour as a cultural education. The typical route included Paris, the Swiss Alps, and the cities of northern Italy — Venice, Florence and Rome. Young men spent months or years abroad, studying art, architecture and antiquities, and returned with Continental tastes and acquired artworks. It was expensive, time-consuming and available only to the elite.

Key Fact

Thomas Cook organised the first commercially promoted railway excursion in 1841 — a trip from Leicester to Loughborough for a temperance rally. He went on to develop package tours to the seaside and eventually abroad, making leisure travel accessible to the middle classes and, later, the working class.

The Railway and the Seaside

The rapid expansion of the railway network after the 1840s transformed the British holiday. Resorts that had previously been accessible only to wealthy visitors who could travel by coach suddenly became reachable in hours from industrial cities. Blackpool, accessible by rail from Manchester and Preston from the 1840s onwards, grew from a small village into a major resort. Brighton, already fashionable among London’s elite, was transformed when the London–Brighton line opened in 1841, cutting the journey to under two hours.

Seaside resorts invested heavily in attractions: piers, promenades, theatres, bandstands and amusement arcades. The railway brought day-trippers and week-long holidaymakers alike. Blackpool built its famous tower in 1894, modelled on the Eiffel Tower. By the late nineteenth century, the seaside holiday had become a defining feature of working-class leisure culture in industrial Britain.

The Bank Holiday Act of 1871, introduced by Sir John Lubbock, created official public holidays — Easter Monday, Whit Monday, the first Monday in August, and Boxing Day. These were not paid holidays for most workers initially, but they established the principle of regular leisure time. Crucially, they coincided with the growth of cheap rail travel, making day trips and short breaks possible for millions.

Paid holidays came later and unevenly. Some workers had negotiated a week’s paid leave by the early twentieth century, but millions had none. The Holidays with Pay Act of 1938 required employers to give workers at least one week’s paid holiday per year — though war interrupted its full implementation. By the 1950s and 1960s, two weeks of paid annual leave was becoming the norm, fundamentally changing the scale of the British holiday market.

Holiday Camps and National Parks

The 1930s saw the rise of the holiday camp. Billy Butlin opened his first camp at Skegness in 1936, offering an all-inclusive holiday at a fixed price. Holiday camps were designed to give working-class families a full week’s holiday without the worry of organising food, accommodation and entertainment separately. By the early 1950s, Butlin’s camps were hosting around a million visitors a year. The holiday camp model represented a new democratisation of the British holiday.

The National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act of 1949 created the first national parks in England and Wales, designating areas of outstanding natural beauty for public enjoyment. The Peak District became the first national park in 1951. Improved bus and car ownership allowed day-trippers and hikers to reach the countryside in growing numbers through the 1950s and 1960s.

Package holidays to the Mediterranean expanded rapidly during the 1960s. Vladimir Raitz of Horizon Holidays organised the first modern package tour to Corsica in 1950, and the market grew quickly once jet aviation made the journey faster. By the early 1970s, millions of British holidaymakers were flying to Spain, Greece and Portugal each year. Low-cost airlines like Ryanair and easyJet, which expanded during the 1990s, further reduced the cost of foreign travel.

The consequence for British seaside resorts was devastating. Blackpool, Skegness, Margate and other traditional resorts faced declining visitor numbers from the 1970s onwards. They struggled to compete with guaranteed sunshine, cheap wine and modern hotels abroad. Some invested in new attractions — Blackpool added a major indoor entertainment complex. Others declined sharply, with high unemployment and derelict seafronts becoming a visible social problem by the 1980s.

Key Fact

The growth of cheap air travel and Mediterranean package holidays from the 1960s fundamentally changed British holiday patterns. Millions chose Spain and Greece over Blackpool and Scarborough. British seaside resorts experienced serious decline: by the 1970s many were losing visitors rapidly to foreign destinations.

Change and Continuity

Tracing holiday patterns from c.500 to the present reveals a clear pattern of gradual widening access. Medieval feast days were universally available but brief; the Grand Tour was exclusive and long. The railway opened the seaside to the urban working class; bank holidays and paid leave formalised leisure time; holiday camps democratised the week-away holiday; package holidays exported British leisure culture to the Mediterranean. Technology — the steam locomotive, the jet aircraft, the budget airline — was the decisive driver of each shift. Throughout, class shaped both what was possible and where people went.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Theatre, stage and screen: medieval to Victorian
content_html:
Viking Sagas and Anglo-Saxon Performance

Long before permanent theatres existed in Britain, sagas and epic poems provided entertainment in the great halls of the early medieval period. Travelling performers — known as scops in Anglo-Saxon culture — recited long narrative poems from memory, accompanied by a harp. The Old English epic poem Beowulf, composed some time between the seventh and tenth centuries, is the most famous surviving example. It tells the story of a Geatish hero who defeats the monster Grendel, and its performance context was the communal hall.

Viking culture brought its own tradition of saga performance to Britain. Norse sagas combined heroic narrative, mythological content and genealogical history. Performance was communal, participatory and central to identity. There were no buildings dedicated to performance: the hall, the church, and later the market square served as informal venues.

Medieval Mystery Plays

Mystery plays were the dominant form of popular drama in medieval England. They dramatised stories from the Bible, from Creation to the Last Judgement, in a cycle of short plays performed by the town guilds on wagons in a sequence of stops around the town centre. The York Mystery Plays and the Chester Mystery Plays are the best-documented surviving cycles. Performances took place on the feast of Corpus Christi, providing religious instruction through entertainment.

The guilds took great pride in their performances: the shipwrights typically played the story of Noah’s Ark; the bakers, the Last Supper. Costumes and props became elaborate, and performances could draw large crowds. Mummers also provided dramatic entertainment, particularly at Christmas: troupes of masked performers enacted folk dramas, often involving a symbolic death-and-resurrection narrative.

Key Fact

Medieval mystery plays were performed on wagons by town guilds on the feast of Corpus Christi. The York and Chester cycles are the most important surviving examples. They combined religious instruction with popular entertainment, making Bible stories accessible to people who could not read.

The Elizabethan Playhouse

The opening of the first permanent public theatre in London — simply called The Theatre — in Shoreditch in 1576 marks a decisive moment in English cultural history. Within two decades, a thriving commercial theatre industry had emerged in the suburbs of London, outside the jurisdiction of the city authorities who disapproved of theatre as immoral and disruptive.

The most famous of the Elizabethan playhouses was the Globe Theatre, built in Southwark in 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain’s Men, the company that included William Shakespeare as both playwright and sharer. The Globe was a large, open-air, three-tiered circular structure accommodating perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 spectators. Admission was as little as a penny for standing room in the pit, making theatre genuinely accessible to ordinary Londoners — apprentices, craftsmen and servant girls attended alongside the wealthy in the galleries.

The plays performed in Elizabethan theatre ranged from Shakespeare’s tragedies and histories to the comedies of Ben Jonson and the tragedies of Christopher Marlowe. Performance depended on spoken language, elaborate costume and convention rather than scenery, because the open-air stage had no ability to change lighting. Cross-dressing was necessary because women were barred from the stage — all female roles were played by boy actors.

The Puritan-dominated Parliament closed all public theatres in 1642 as ungodly and disruptive. They remained closed for eighteen years. When Charles II was restored to the throne in 1660, he brought back a taste for European theatrical culture, including painted scenery, indoor candlelit theatres and, for the first time, professional women actors on the English stage. Restoration theatre was initially an elite affair, attracting the court and the fashionable classes, but it gradually spread to broader urban audiences.

Victorian Music Halls

The music hall was the defining entertainment venue of Victorian Britain. Growing out of pub concert rooms in the 1840s, dedicated music hall buildings were constructed across British towns and cities. By 1866, London alone had around 30 large music halls and over 200 smaller venues. The entertainment was fast-paced, populist and participatory: comic singers, acrobats, jugglers, magicians and sentimental balladeers performed in rotation before audiences who ate, drank and sang along.

Star performers became the celebrities of their age. Marie Lloyd, whose career reached its peak in the 1890s, was one of the most famous music hall entertainers in Britain, known for comic songs with risqué undertones that commented on working-class life. Albert Chevalier and Dan Leno were equally celebrated. Music halls provided the model for later variety theatre, the circus, and ultimately the format of television light entertainment.

Alongside music halls, glee clubs represented a more respectable strand of musical entertainment. They originated in the eighteenth century as male singing societies, performing harmonised part-songs. By the nineteenth century the tradition had broadened: choral societies proliferated across industrial towns, particularly in the north and Wales. The Huddersfield Choral Society, founded in 1836, is one of the most famous surviving examples. Choral singing gave working-class people a respected cultural activity that crossed religious and political lines.

Key Fact

Music halls were Victorian variety entertainment venues that grew from pub concert rooms in the 1840s. By the 1860s London had over 200 such venues. Stars like Marie Lloyd became nationally celebrated. Music halls were the dominant popular entertainment of the late Victorian period until the rise of cinema.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Cinema, TV and screen entertainment from 1920
content_html:
The Arrival of Cinema

Moving pictures reached British audiences at the end of the nineteenth century. The Lumière brothers demonstrated their Cinématographe in London in February 1896, and purpose-built cinemas began to appear in British towns and cities from around 1907. Early silent films were short, simple and accompanied by a piano or organ played live in the cinema. By the early 1920s, cinema had become the most popular form of mass entertainment in Britain, particularly for working-class urban audiences.

The 1920s saw the construction of purpose-built “picture palaces” — large, ornate cinemas designed to offer audiences a glamorous escape from everyday life. By the mid-1930s, the United Kingdom had around 4,300 cinemas with a combined weekly attendance of approximately 18-20 million. Going to the pictures was a regular weekly habit for millions of British people, particularly for young adults and courting couples.

Key Fact

The talkies arrived when the American film The Jazz Singer was released in 1927, featuring synchronised speech and song. British cinemas quickly converted to sound equipment, and audiences grew even larger. The 1930s were the golden age of British cinema attendance.

British Cinema in the 1930s and 1940s

Hollywood dominated, but British cinema had its own identity. Ealing Studios produced a distinctive strand of British comedy and drama from the late 1930s onwards, culminating in the classic Ealing comedies of the late 1940s and early 1950s — films such as Passport to Pimlico (1949), Kind Hearts and Coronets (1949), and The Lavender Hill Mob (1951). These films reflected British culture, humour and social anxieties in ways that American films could not.

Cinema attendance peaked in Britain in 1946 at approximately 1.64 billion tickets sold in a single year — equivalent to an average of about 31 visits per person per year. This figure illustrates how central cinema had become to British social life in the immediate post-war period. The cinema was warm, cheap, and offered two hours of escapism from the austerity of post-war Britain.

The BBC launched the world’s first regular public television service from Alexandra Palace in November 1936. The service was suspended during the Second World War and resumed in June 1946. Television ownership grew slowly at first because sets were expensive. The 1953 coronation of Queen Elizabeth II was the decisive moment that drove mass television adoption: an estimated 20 million people watched it in Britain, most on sets owned by neighbours or in public venues.

ITV (Independent Television) launched in September 1955, breaking the BBC’s monopoly and introducing commercial broadcasting. Competition improved programming quality and drove up television ownership. Colour television was introduced on BBC2 in 1967 and on BBC1 and ITV in 1969. By 1971, colour licences outnumbered black-and-white ones for the first time.

Cinema’s Decline and Television’s Dominance

The relationship between cinema and television was initially competitive, and cinema lost. British cinema admissions fell from 1.64 billion in 1946 to around 501 million in 1960, and to approximately 194 million by 1970. Hundreds of cinemas closed; many were converted into bingo halls. Television, free at the point of use (after the initial set cost and licence fee), available at home and increasingly offering a wide range of content, was simply more convenient.

Cinema survived by differentiating itself: large screens, better sound, and ultimately blockbuster films that could not be replicated at home. The invention of the VCR (video cassette recorder) in the late 1970s and its mass adoption in the 1980s seemed to threaten cinemas further, but in fact the two co-existed as the appetite for screen entertainment grew. Cinema admissions have broadly recovered since the 1990s, driven by multiplex development, blockbuster franchises and digital presentation.

The late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries brought further transformation. Digital recording, the DVD, and then broadband internet changed how people consumed screen entertainment again. Streaming services such as Netflix (available in the UK from 2012) and later Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video changed viewing habits fundamentally. By the early 2020s, streaming had overtaken traditional broadcast television as the primary way many younger viewers consumed screen entertainment.

The shift to on-demand, personalised viewing represents a significant break with the shared experience that had defined cinema and television from the 1920s to the 1990s. Instead of a nation watching the same programme at the same time, audiences fragmented into millions of individual choices. The social experience of “going to the pictures” or gathering round the television for a shared broadcast became rarer, though blockbuster cinema events retained their communal appeal.

Key Fact

The 1953 coronation of Queen Elizabeth II was watched by approximately 20 million people in Britain and was the decisive moment that drove mass adoption of television. Cinema admissions had already peaked in 1946 at around 1.64 billion, and the rise of television accelerated their rapid decline through the 1950s and 1960s.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Music and dance over time
content_html:
Medieval and Religious Music

The dominant musical tradition of medieval Europe was plainchant, also known as Gregorian chant after Pope Gregory I, who is traditionally credited with organising the repertoire in the late sixth century. Sung by monks and clergy in Latin, plainchant was the foundation of liturgical worship in monasteries and churches across England. It was not entertainment in a modern sense, but it shaped the entire musical culture of the medieval period.

Outside the monastery, travelling musicians — known as minstrels or jongleurs — provided entertainment at feasts, fairs and markets. They sang ballads and narrative songs, played instruments such as the lute, viol and pipe, and accompanied dancing. Music was inseparable from dance in the medieval period: communal dance was a feature of village festivals, wedding celebrations and harvest feasts.

Tudor Courtly Music and the Reformation

Under the Tudor monarchs, courtly music flourished. Henry VIII was himself a musician and composer, credited with composing “Pastime with Good Company.” Courtly music at the Tudor court included polyphonic vocal compositions, lute songs, and dance music for the consort. Professional musicians held court appointments and were among the best-paid royal servants.

The Protestant Reformation of the 1530s and 1540s had profound effects on English musical culture. The dissolution of the monasteries removed the institutional basis of plainchant. Protestant worship emphasised congregational singing in English rather than Latin choir music. Thomas Cranmer’s first Book of Common Prayer in 1549 standardised English liturgical practice and eventually gave rise to new traditions of hymn singing.

The eighteenth century saw the development of orchestral and classical music as a public entertainment. George Frideric Handel, a German-born composer who spent much of his career in London, was central to English musical life. His oratorios — including Messiah, first performed in Dublin in 1742 — attracted large audiences and established a tradition of choral performance that has continued ever since. Public concerts in purpose-built venues, subscription series and music rooms became fashionable from the 1720s and 1730s.

Pleasure gardens such as Vauxhall Gardens in London provided outdoor musical entertainment for mixed social audiences. Orchestral performances, fireworks, illuminations and popular songs all featured. The pleasure garden combined the social functions of the park, the concert hall and the theatre in a single venue.

Key Fact

Brass bands became a major form of communal musical culture in nineteenth-century industrial Britain, particularly in the north of England and Wales. Colliery bands, factory bands and Salvation Army bands provided music at community events, competitions and religious gatherings. The first Brass Band Championship was held in 1853.

The Radio Age and Popular Music

The BBC began regular radio broadcasts in 1922, transforming how ordinary people listened to music. For the first time, professional music performances could reach the entire country simultaneously without the audience leaving home. Jazz was introduced to British audiences partly through radio and partly through American musicians touring Britain in the 1920s. Dance halls playing jazz and big band music became enormously popular: the Hammersmith Palais, which opened in 1919, was one of hundreds of dedicated dance venues that opened across Britain in the interwar years.

Rock and roll arrived in Britain from America in the mid-1950s. Bill Haley and His Comets’ “Rock Around the Clock” reached the UK charts in 1955 and was associated with a new youth culture — the teenager. Elvis Presley’s recordings reached British audiences from 1956. British musicians quickly created their own rock and roll: Tommy Steele was one of the first successful British rock performers from 1956.

In 1964, the Beatles toured the United States and triggered what became known as the “British Invasion” — a wave of British pop and rock acts that dominated American charts, including the Rolling Stones, the Kinks and the Who. British pop music had become a globally significant cultural export. The transistor radio, cheap and portable, had made pop music accessible anywhere; teenagers in the 1960s carried music with them in a way that earlier generations could not.

The 1970s brought punk rock as a reaction against mainstream pop; the 1980s saw synthesiser-based pop and the rise of MTV; the 1990s produced Britpop acts including Oasis, Blur and Pulp. Each decade’s popular music reflected social and economic conditions. By the 2000s, digital downloading and then streaming via services like Spotify (launched 2006, available in UK from 2008) had fundamentally changed how music was distributed and consumed.

Key Fact

How people listened to music changed dramatically across the twentieth century: BBC radio (1922) brought professional music into the home; the transistor radio (1950s–1960s) made listening portable; the record player and LP allowed home listening on demand; digital streaming from the 2000s gave instant access to millions of tracks. Each technology both democratised music and changed its commercial structure.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Children's entertainment over time
content_html:
Medieval and Early Modern Children’s Play

Children’s play in medieval England was less clearly separated from adult activity than it is today. Young children had simple toys made from available materials: wooden horses and carts, clay figures, cloth dolls, and spinning tops. Archaeological excavations of medieval sites have recovered such objects, confirming that play was a recognised part of childhood. Children also participated in adult games and festivals from an early age.

In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, toys became somewhat more elaborate but remained homemade or locally crafted. Hobby horses — simple wooden sticks with a carved horse’s head — were among the most common children’s playthings recorded in sources from this period. Boys played versions of football and wrestling alongside adults; girls were more typically directed towards domestic activities and needlework, though they too played with dolls and participated in communal games on feast days.

Key Fact

Victorian industrialisation transformed children’s toys. Factory-produced toys became available for the first time, including tin trains, mechanical toys, wooden building blocks and porcelain dolls. The introduction of compulsory education from 1870 and growing middle-class prosperity drove demand for educational and recreational toys. Wealthy children could afford elaborate toy trains and dolls’ houses; poorer children still made do with homemade objects.

Victorian and Edwardian Comics

The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw the development of illustrated magazines and comics aimed at children. The comics industry grew alongside mass literacy, as the Education Act of 1870 brought compulsory schooling for all children. Comics offered affordable weekly entertainment: titles aimed at boys typically featured adventure, sport and humour, while girls’ comics emphasised friendship, home and romance.

The Beano launched in 1938 and the Dandy in 1937 — both published by D.C. Thomson in Dundee — became the most enduring British children’s comics of the twentieth century. The Eagle, launched in 1950 by clergyman Marcus Morris, targeted older boys with its distinctive combination of science fiction (Dan Dare, Pilot of the Future), adventure strips and educational content. At its peak in the 1950s, the Eagle sold nearly a million copies a week.

BBC radio provided dedicated children’s programming from its early years. Children’s Hour, first broadcast in 1922, offered stories, drama and music for younger listeners, and ran until 1961. Listen with Mother, aimed at the youngest children, ran from 1950 to 1982. When television reached British homes in the 1950s, children’s programming transferred quickly to the new medium.

Blue Peter launched on the BBC in October 1958 and has run continuously since, making it one of the longest-running children’s television programmes in the world. Watch with Mother (1950–1980) served pre-school children with puppet programmes including The Flowerpot Men and The Wooden Tops. Children’s television became a significant part of the BBC’s public service remit, providing programming that was both entertaining and educational.

The Video Game Revolution

The late twentieth century saw a new form of children’s entertainment that was interactive in a way no previous medium had been. Video games arrived in British homes with the Atari 2600 in the late 1970s and the rise of home computers such as the ZX Spectrum (1982) and the Commodore 64 (1982). Nintendo’s Game Boy (1989) and its console systems brought new levels of sophistication; the Sony PlayStation (1995) and its successors brought cinematic-quality graphics.

By the early 2000s, video games had become the dominant leisure activity for many children and teenagers. The industry’s global revenue surpassed that of cinema by the early twenty-first century. Games also changed the nature of play: it became more solitary and screen-based, and it extended into adulthood in a way that traditional children’s toys did not.

One of the most significant changes in children’s leisure from the late twentieth century was the decline of outdoor, unsupervised play. In the 1970s, a typical British child walked or cycled to school, played freely in the street or on waste ground, and ranged relatively widely without adult supervision. By the 2000s, parental fears about road traffic and stranger danger had dramatically reduced this freedom. Research by Play England found that children’s “home range” — the area within which they were allowed to roam freely — had shrunk by approximately 90% between the 1970s and the 2000s.

Key Fact

By the start of the twenty-first century, children’s leisure had shifted decisively from outdoor, unsupervised, physical play to indoor, screen-based, often solitary activities. This represented a radical break with centuries of tradition, in which children’s play had been primarily communal, physical and outdoor. The change was driven by technology, rising parental anxiety, traffic, and the entertainment industry’s targeting of children as consumers.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Cruelty in sport and entertainment
content_html:
Medieval Hunting and Violence as Entertainment

In medieval England, the boundary between sport and violence was very different from today’s. Hunting was simultaneously a food source, a military training exercise and a leisure activity, but the suffering of animals was an accepted part of it. Bull-baiting attracted large crowds in towns and villages. A bull was chained to a stake and dogs set against it; the contest could last for hours. Cockfighting, bear-baiting and badger-baiting were similarly popular. None of these activities was considered cruel in the modern sense — animal suffering was simply not a significant moral category in medieval or early modern thinking.

Public executions served a similar function. Executions at the gallows at Tyburn (near present-day Marble Arch in London) attracted enormous crowds. Public hangings, drawings and quarterings were organised as spectacles designed to deter crime and demonstrate royal justice. The crowd was expected to participate: cheering, jeering, throwing food, and sometimes rescuing condemned individuals who had popular sympathy. These events were understood as entertainment as well as punishment.

Key Fact

The Cruelty to Animals Act of 1835 prohibited bull-baiting, bear-baiting and cockfighting in Britain. This followed earlier failed attempts to legislate against animal cruelty and reflected the growing influence of middle-class reformers who argued that cruelty to animals brutalised human beings and damaged public morality.

Bare-Knuckle Prizefighting

Prizefighting — bare-knuckle boxing for money — was enormously popular in eighteenth and early nineteenth-century England, drawing large crowds and heavy gambling. Matches were essentially unregulated: there were no rounds of fixed length, no weight categories, and fights continued until one man could not continue. The sport attracted significant violence outside the ring as well — brawls between partisan crowds were common.

The introduction of formal rules transformed boxing. The London Prize Ring rules of 1838 introduced some structure, but the decisive change came in 1867 when the Marquess of Queensberry rules introduced gloves, three-minute rounds and a ten-second count for knocked-down fighters. These rules formed the basis of modern amateur and professional boxing and gradually replaced the bare-knuckle tradition by the 1890s.

The Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) was founded in 1824, originally as the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. It gained its royal charter in 1840. The RSPCA reflected a significant shift in middle-class Victorian attitudes: the view that animals could suffer in a morally meaningful way, and that inflicting unnecessary suffering was wrong regardless of its entertainment value.

This change in attitude drew on Evangelical Christian thinking about responsibility for the created world, and on the emerging sciences of animal physiology that demonstrated that animals felt pain in ways similar to humans. By the mid-Victorian period, bull-baiting and cockfighting were increasingly associated with the “rougher” elements of the working class and condemned by respectable middle-class opinion as degrading.

Fox Hunting and the Modern Debate

Fox hunting on horseback, with hounds, became the dominant rural sport of the English upper and middle classes from the eighteenth century onwards. Unlike bull-baiting, fox hunting was never subjected to the same reformist pressure in the Victorian era because its practitioners were politically powerful and argued that it was pest control as well as sport. Fox hunting became an important part of rural social life, with hunts organising the social calendar of many country communities.

Serious legislative debate about fox hunting began in the 1960s, driven by the League Against Cruel Sports (founded 1924) and growing urban opinion that the sport was cruel and anachronistic. A series of private members’ bills attempted to ban hunting in the 1990s. The Burns Inquiry, published in 2000, examined the evidence about the suffering involved and the economic impact of a ban. Its findings were deliberately cautious on whether hunting was cruel, but it did conclude that hunting caused “serious welfare concerns.”

The Hunting Act of 2004 banned hunting wild mammals with dogs in England and Wales. It came into force in February 2005. The bill passed after a long parliamentary battle, including the use of the Parliament Acts to overcome House of Lords opposition. Supporters argued it ended unnecessary animal suffering; opponents argued it was an attack on rural traditions and a class-based assault on country sports.

The Hunting Act 2004 represents the modern end of the long story of cruelty in sport: a trajectory that began with the Cruelty to Animals Act 1835, continued with the regulation of boxing under the Queensberry rules, and reflected a fundamental shift in public attitudes towards the rights and welfare of animals over more than 150 years. Animal rights organisations such as the League Against Cruel Sports continue to campaign for stricter enforcement.

Key Fact

Legislation progressively restricted cruel sports: the Cruelty to Animals Act 1835 banned bull-baiting and cockfighting; the Marquess of Queensberry rules (1867) reformed boxing; the Hunting Act 2004 banned fox hunting with dogs. Each change reflected shifting middle-class and public attitudes towards animal welfare, reinforced by organised campaigns from the RSPCA and the League Against Cruel Sports.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Historic environment: Glastonbury Festival c.1970 to the present day
content_html:
The Origins of Glastonbury Festival

Glastonbury Festival began on a Somerset dairy farm. Worthy Farm, owned by dairy farmer Michael Eavis, hosted the first event on 19 September 1970, the day after Jimi Hendrix died. It was called the Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival. Around 1,500 people attended and paid one pound, which included free milk from the farm. The event had a small makeshift stage; the atmosphere was informal, communal and countercultural.

The following year, in 1971, a larger event took place under the name Glastonbury Fayre. This event was influenced by the idealism of the late 1960s counterculture: free admission was charged, alternative therapies and crafts were offered alongside music, and the event was associated with hippie values and the idea of a natural, communal gathering. T. Rex headlined in 1971; David Bowie played the Pyramid Stage in 1971 as well, giving an early morning performance that has passed into festival legend.

Key Fact

The first Glastonbury event took place on 19 September 1970, organised by Michael Eavis at Worthy Farm, Pilton, Somerset. Approximately 1,500 people attended and paid one pound each, including free milk. It was called the Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival. The modern festival grew from this small, informal beginning.

The Pyramid Stage and Early Growth

The Pyramid Stage was first constructed in 1971 by Bill Harkin, a designer influenced by the alternative architecture movement. Built from scaffolding covered in a polythene skin and shaped as a pyramid — reportedly aligned with the Cheops pyramid — it gave the festival a striking visual identity that persisted through multiple rebuilds. The current Pyramid Stage is a large permanent steel structure, but its distinctive shape remains.

The festival did not run every year in its early decades. It was held intermittently in the early 1970s, and became an annual event from 1981. During the 1980s, the festival grew steadily in size and ambition. It gained a reputation not only for music but for its eclectic mix of theatre, circus, cabaret, healing fields and market stalls. It also developed a distinctive political character: the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) received a portion of the profits for many years from 1981.

The early 1990s exposed serious problems. The growth of the illegal rave and free party movement meant that Glastonbury became a magnet for large numbers of gatecrashers and festival-goers who had not paid. The 1992 festival saw estimated crowds of 70,000–80,000, far exceeding the licenced capacity, and there were significant public order concerns. Security became a serious issue throughout the mid-1990s.

The installation of the famous “Super Fence” — a steel perimeter fence several miles long — in 2002 transformed the festival’s physical form. The fence ended the tradition of free entry for those who could not afford a ticket or climbed in without paying. It made Glastonbury a secure, ticketed event with defined entrances. Critics argued it destroyed the festival’s countercultural spirit; supporters argued it saved the event from being shut down by the local council and police.

Glastonbury in the Twenty-First Century

By the 2000s, Glastonbury had established itself as the world’s largest greenfield music festival. Attendance regularly exceeded 200,000. The festival adopted a fallow year system — years with no festival — to allow the farmland to recover. Fallow years occurred in 1991, 1996, 2001 (foot-and-mouth disease), 2006, 2012, and 2018. The absence of a festival heightened demand and reinforced the event’s special character.

The programme diversified significantly. Dance music, which had been marginal in the early years, gained its own dedicated spaces in the 1990s and 2000s, including the Dance Village and the Park Stage. The “Legends Slot” — a Sunday afternoon performance by a veteran or legacy artist — became one of the most watched moments of each festival, featuring artists such as Shirley Bassey (2007), Paul McCartney (2004), and David Bowie (2000). The BBC began broadcasting extensive live footage from Glastonbury in the late 1990s, extending its audience far beyond the site itself.

Glastonbury connects to the broader themes of entertainment and leisure across the full period. It is a modern version of a tradition of communal, outdoor festivity that stretches back to medieval feast days and harvest festivals. Like the medieval fair, it combines music, performance, trade and community gathering in a rural setting. Like the Victorian music hall, it made entertainment accessible to large numbers of people — though now a ticket costs hundreds of pounds rather than a shilling.

The festival’s history also illustrates key themes of change: the shift from countercultural idealism (1970s free admission) to commercial spectacle (2000s sold-out ticketed event with corporate sponsorship); the impact of broadcasting technology (BBC coverage from the late 1990s turning a local Somerset event into a national cultural institution); and the tension between mass participation and exclusive access (the fencing controversy of 2002). It is a microcosm of how British popular entertainment changed over the twentieth century.

Key Fact

Glastonbury Festival links to the wider thematic study in two ways: it is a continuation of the tradition of communal outdoor festivity (medieval fairs, harvest festivals); and it shows the modern tension between accessible popular entertainment and commercial exclusivity. BBC coverage from the late 1990s and streaming from the 2010s transformed a local Somerset event into a global cultural institution.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Themes: continuity and change in British entertainment
content_html:
Why Did Entertainment and Leisure Change?

Across 1,500 years of British history, entertainment and leisure were shaped by a small number of recurring forces. Historians typically group these into four categories: factors driving change. Understanding these factors is essential for the 16-mark thematic change essay, which requires you not just to describe what changed but to explain why.

These four factors did not work independently — they interacted. Religious reform changed attitudes to violence in sport; those changed attitudes enabled legislation; legislation reflected and reinforced changing wealth distribution; technology created new forms of entertainment that bypassed older restrictions. The most sophisticated analysis traces these interactions across the three eras.

Factor 1: Technology

Technology has been the most consistent driver of change in leisure and entertainment across the whole period. In each major era, a new technology opened up entertainment to larger numbers of people and changed both what was available and how people consumed it.

In the early modern period, the printing press (introduced to England by William Caxton in 1476) made written entertainment possible for the literate classes and eventually for the mass market. In the modern era: the steam railway (1840s onwards) allowed seaside holidays; the cinema (from 1896) provided mass entertainment; the radio (BBC from 1922) brought professional music and drama into every home; the television (BBC from 1936) created a new national shared culture; the internet and streaming have disaggregated that shared culture into millions of individual choices. Each of these technologies produced a step-change in access.

Key Fact

Technology drove the most dramatic changes in entertainment access: the railway (1840s) democratised holidays; cinema (1896) created mass entertainment; radio (1922) brought professional performance to every home; television (BBC 1936) created shared national culture; internet and streaming (2000s) fragmented viewing into personalised on-demand consumption.

Factor 2: Wealth and Income

Throughout the period, access to leisure was shaped by income. In the medieval period, the jousting tournament, falconry and the Grand Tour were available only to those with significant wealth. The railway seaside holiday was initially middle-class; it became accessible to the working class only as rail fares fell and Saturday half-holidays freed up time. Holiday camps (1930s) and then package holidays (1960s) extended cheap leisure further down the income scale.

Rising real wages in the twentieth century — particularly in the post-war boom years of the 1950s and 1960s — expanded the leisure market dramatically. More people had more money and more time. Consumer capitalism created new leisure industries. The idea that every household should have a television, then a video recorder, then a games console, was driven as much by economic aspiration as by technological possibility.

Government and legislation shaped leisure in two contradictory ways: restricting some activities and expanding access to others. The Norman Forest Laws (post-1066) restricted hunting; Edward III’s 1363 proclamation tried to ban football; the Puritan Parliament closed theatres in 1642. Each of these was an attempt to control popular leisure for religious, military or moral reasons.

In contrast, from the nineteenth century onwards, government increasingly acted to expand leisure access: the Bank Holiday Act 1871 created public holidays; the Holidays with Pay Act 1938 gave workers a legal right to paid leave; the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949 opened up the countryside; the Cruelty to Animals Act 1835 and the Hunting Act 2004 ended cruel sports. This shift from restriction to facilitation reflects a broader change in how governments understood their role in social life.

Religion and moral attitudes have repeatedly reshaped what forms of entertainment were permitted. The medieval Church shaped the leisure calendar through feast days; Protestant reformers condemned dancing, drama and sport as ungodly; Victorian Evangelicalism drove the reform of cruel sports; the relaxation of Sunday trading laws in 1994 reflected secularisation. Each shift in religious authority reshaped what people were allowed and expected to do in their leisure time.

Changing attitudes — not just formal religion — also mattered. The shift in public attitudes towards animal welfare between 1800 and 2004 was driven partly by religion (Evangelical concern for creation) but also by science (animal physiology showing that animals felt pain) and by class politics (middle-class rejection of “rough” working-class pastimes). Attitudes towards women in sport, children’s unsupervised play, and gambling have all shifted in ways that reshaped entertainment provision.

What Stayed the Same?

Alongside all this change, some fundamental continuities are visible. Entertainment has always been communal at its heart: from the medieval feast to the Victorian music hall to Glastonbury Festival, people have sought leisure in company. Sport has always been tied to physical skill, competition and communal identity — the village football match and the Premier League are separated by 700 years but share the same underlying human drives. Class has consistently shaped access to the best forms of leisure, even as the definition of “the best” has changed. And each generation has used new technologies to do what previous generations did with older ones: tell stories, make music, watch spectacle, and belong to something larger than themselves.

Key Fact

The four main drivers of change in British entertainment were technology, wealth and income, government and legislation, and religion and changing attitudes. The most significant continuity across the whole period was the communal nature of entertainment: from medieval feast days to modern festivals, people have sought leisure together, not alone.

unit_name: Changes in Entertainment and Leisure in Britain, c.500 to the present day
lesson_title: Exam technique: thematic change essays
content_html:
What the 16-Mark Essay Demands

The 16-mark thematic change essay is the most demanding question in this unit. It carries 16 marks and rewards students who can sustain an analytical argument across the full sweep of British history, from the medieval period to the present day. The question will typically be a statement about change or continuity — for example, “Technology was the main reason why entertainment changed in Britain” or “Entertainment became more accessible throughout the period” — and will ask “How far do you agree?”

The key requirements are: evidence from all three eras (medieval c.500–1500, early modern c.1500–1850, and modern c.1850–present); a clear argument that weighs change against continuity; and a substantiated overall judgement. Students who cover only one era, or who list events without arguing a case, cap themselves at the lower bands.

Key Fact

A thematic change essay on entertainment must cover all three eras: medieval (c.500–1500: feast days, jousting, mystery plays, village games); early modern (c.1500–1850: Tudor hunting, Elizabethan theatre, Grand Tour, brass bands); and modern (c.1850–present: spectator sport, cinema, radio, television, streaming). Missing an era costs access to the top bands.

How to Structure Your Essay

A strong thematic change essay has a clear structure. One effective approach is to organise by second-order concepts: write about what changed, then what stayed the same, then reach an overall judgement. Another approach is to organise by factor (technology, then wealth, then government) while weaving evidence from all three eras into each section.

Whatever structure you choose, every paragraph should follow a clear pattern: make a point, support it with specific evidence, explain what it shows about change or continuity, and link back to the question. Paragraphs that only describe events without explaining their significance for change or continuity will not access the top bands.

Examiners consistently identify the same errors in weaker essays. First: covering only one era. Many students write entirely about the modern period (cinema, television, streaming) and miss the medieval and early modern content entirely. This caps the response in the middle band, regardless of how good the modern content is.

Second: describing change rather than explaining it. A response that says “Sport changed a lot in Victorian Britain because football was codified in 1863 and the FA Cup started in 1872” is describing, not explaining. The examiner wants to know why sport changed: what caused codification? (Public schools, railways, Saturday half-holiday, urban growth.) The description scores the knowledge mark; the explanation earns the analysis mark.

Third: no overall judgement. Many students end their essay with the last piece of evidence rather than a conclusion. A conclusion must do more than summarise: it must state how much things changed, whether change was progressive or uneven, and what the most significant factor was. Even a single well-argued final sentence earns judgement marks.

Worked Example Opening

Question: “Technology was the main reason why entertainment changed so much in Britain between c.500 and the present day.” How far do you agree?

A Mastering-level opening might begin:

“Technology was undoubtedly a powerful force for change in British entertainment across the period: the railway from the 1840s democratised the seaside holiday; the cinema (from 1896) created mass entertainment; the radio (BBC 1922) and television (BBC 1936) brought professional performance into every home; and internet streaming from the 2000s has fragmented national culture into personalised individual consumption. However, technology alone does not explain change: in the medieval period, feast days and mystery plays provided communal entertainment with no new technology at all — their organisation depended on the Church and the guild system. The most important single turning point was arguably the steam railway, which simultaneously democratised leisure time (making the seaside possible) and laid the infrastructure for the modern mass entertainment industry.”

Notice what this opening does: it immediately engages with the question, provides evidence from all three eras, and signals both agreement and a challenge. It sets up the argument without simply listing facts.

Your conclusion must state a clear overall judgement. It should answer the question directly: “How far do you agree?” The best conclusions weigh the evidence, acknowledge the strongest counter-argument, and still come down on one side. For example: “Technology was the most important single driver of change in entertainment, but it worked through other factors: without rising wages and paid leave, most people could not afford the new technologies; without legislation, neither the railway nor the cinema would have operated safely. Change was uneven — dramatic in the modern era, far slower in the medieval and early modern periods — because only modern technology could reach the majority of the population.”

Key Fact

The four ingredients of a top-band thematic change essay are: evidence from all three eras; a clear argument about change AND continuity; explanation of why things changed (not just what changed); and a substantiated overall judgement in the conclusion. Any essay missing one of these ingredients cannot reach the top band.
